column4: The command to give women their ṣaduqāt as a free gift places the source section's secondary ṣ-d-q sense, bridal due, and the surah's act of giving in one concrete marriage scene.
The single soul's mate, sexual covering in تَغَشَّاهَا, pregnancy, and the couple's request for a sound child enact the section's full movement from covering to conception and promised gratitude.
After the child is given, the couple associates partners in the gift; paired with 7:189, this is the section's broken parental promise, while فَتَعَالَى reaches the same height-root as al-Aʿlā.
Fasting nights permit marital approach, call each spouse the other's garment, and end when the white dawn-thread separates from the black, joining sexual covering to daylight's disclosure.
خَلَقَ ٱلزَّوْجَيْنِ ٱلذَّكَرَ وَٱلْأُنثَىٰ restates almost exactly the oath-image of the Creator making the male-female pair.
Immediately after the male-female pair in 53:45, this ayah locates it in an emitted drop, making the section's transition from pairing to generation explicit.
Pregnant women's term ends when they lay down their burden, and the ayah then promises yusr to whoever has taqwā, directly joining delivery, fear of God, and ease as the section does.
Creation from a drop followed by divine measuring, خَلَقَهُۥ فَقَدَّرَهُۥ, supplies the section's womb-stage and its claim that created life is fitted and apportioned.
After creation and measuring in 80:19, ثُمَّ ٱلسَّبِيلَ يَسَّرَهُۥ makes the way easy, allowing the section to hear both emergence from the womb and the path of life.
Imran's wife vows the unborn child in her womb to God, providing the faithful prenatal promise against which the couple's broken promise in 7:189-190 can be read.
The mother delivers a female and voices a male-female distinction, but God's intervening knowledge and Mary's naming prevent her femaleness from fixing her worth.
God accepts the girl with a beautiful acceptance, gives her beautiful growth, and provides for her, completing 3:36's reversal of disappointment at a female birth.
God's gift is stated with daughters first and sons second, making either sex a divine bestowal rather than a scale of ease, honor, or misfortune.
The continuation gives some both males and females and makes others barren, completing 42:49's claim that sex and fertility are apportioned by divine knowledge and power.
A mother carries and delivers her child in hardship, making real labor-pain grounds for gratitude to her while refusing to attach that hardship specifically to a daughter.
The face of the man given news of a female child turns black as he suppresses grief, staging exactly the gendered value scale that the section says the surah dislodges.
The man hides from people and deliberates whether to keep the girl in humiliation or bury her, carrying 16:58's darkened face into the social violence of the preference.
The sequence from drop to clot to مُضْغَةٍ مُّخَلَّقَةٍ, retention in wombs, and birth names the formed flesh-piece behind the section's dictionary sense of creation.
The human begins as an emitted drop, opening a compact creation sequence that reaches the male-female pair in 75:39.
The drop becomes a clot and God creates and proportions it, linking embryonic formation to the section's خَلَقَ before 75:39 names the two sexes.
God makes from the embryo ٱلزَّوْجَيْنِ ٱلذَّكَرَ وَٱلْأُنثَىٰ, directly tying sexual difference to one created origin rather than to opposed value.
One soul, its mate, and creation stage after stage in three darknesses combine pairing, formation, womb, and covering in a single ayah.
One soul and its mate become many men and women, while the ayah invokes the wombs, connecting the pair's creation to kinship generated through birth.
Creation from dust and a drop, making pairs, and the rule that no female conceives or delivers outside God's knowledge unite the section's creation, sex, and womb scenes.
No female conceives or gives birth except with God's knowledge; the hidden reproductive event is thus held within divine knowing rather than human valuation.
God knows what every female bears, every contraction and increase of the womb, and holds everything by measure, directly developing the section's hidden and measured formation.
Divorced women may not conceal what God has created in their wombs, joining hidden pregnancy, divine creation, and the marital boundary within one legal scene.
The drop is placed in a firm lodging, giving the womb-stage that 23:14 then unfolds into successive acts of creation.
The clot, flesh-piece, bones, flesh, and another creation expand the section's formed mudgha into a sequence of divine shaping.
Creation from a lowly fluid begins a four-ayah womb-and-measure sequence that answers the section's question of how male and female life begins.
The fluid is placed in a secure lodging, supplying the protected and hidden womb-space developed by the section.
The womb lodging holds the fluid until a known term, adding temporal measure to the hidden formation.
The closing claim that God determined the process well makes divine measuring the governing action of 77:20-22.
God's question, 'We created you,' makes the Creator rather than the parents the speaker over the reproductive scene developed in the next two ayat.
The emitted seed is placed before the addressee as an observable act, matching the section's movement from union toward birth.
The question whether humans create the seed or God is the Creator locates agency behind conception exactly where the oath to the Creator of male and female does.
The messenger announces that a pure boy will be bestowed on Mary, making a child explicitly a divine gift while opening a birth outside ordinary coupling.
Mary's question that no man has touched her marks a boundary to the section's ordinary movement from male-female union to conception.
The virgin birth is easy for God, a decreed sign and mercy, relocating ease in divine power rather than in the sex of the child.
Mary conceives and withdraws to a distant place, moving the exceptional conception of 19:20-21 into an actual pregnancy.
Labor drives Mary to the palm trunk and makes her wish she had been forgotten; a son's birth is thus the Qur'an's clearest reversal of the proverb that links boys with easy labor.
At the point of severe labor, Mary is consoled and given water, beginning the provision that meets rather than denies birth's hardship.
Fresh dates are made available to Mary during labor, adding bodily provision to the consolation of 19:24.
Husbands must house pregnant divorcees, spend on them until delivery, and pay for nursing, translating the section's gift and birth images into material duty.
After commanding expenditure in the pregnancy context of 65:6, the ayah promises that God will make ease after hardship, joining giving, ʿusr, and yusr.
The mother's weakness upon weakness in carrying and weaning grounds gratitude in the cost of maternity without assigning that cost by the child's sex.
God brings people from their mothers' wombs knowing nothing and gives hearing, sight, and hearts so they may be grateful, joining birth as gift with the gratitude promised in 7:189.
Charitable men and charitable women give God a good loan and receive multiplication; the ṣ-d-q family, giving, ḥusnā-like goodness, and both sexes share one moral measure.
Creation from a male and a female culminates in the declaration that honor is measured by taqwā, directly replacing inherited sex-ranking with the section's moral criterion.
God wastes no deed of any worker, male or female, because each is of the other, explicitly denying that sex determines the outcome of striving.
Men and women are paired across submission, truthfulness, patience, charity, fasting, chastity, and remembrance, then given the same forgiveness and reward.
Every fruit is made a pair and night covers day in the same ayah, a close Qur'anic meeting of the section's paired creation and غ ش و covering.
'We created you in pairs' gives the human-pair premise immediately before the passage turns to sleep, night, and day.
Night is made a garment, echoing both the covering oath and the spouses-as-garments scene of 2:187 after 78:8's creation in pairs.
Day is made for livelihood after night as garment, completing the pair's alternation from covering to an opened field of action.
Day is sworn by when it reveals the sun, using ج ل و for the same daylight unveiling that the section hears as bridal disclosure.
Night is sworn by when it covers the sun, placing the غ ش و counter-action directly beside 91:3's unveiling.
Moses asks to look and God تَجَلَّىٰ to the mountain; manifestation and attempted sight give the section's bridal 'unveiling so the husband looks' a weighty contrasting use of the same root.
The command to glorify the name of the Lord al-Aʿlā takes up the section's final height-word and introduces the creation-guidance sequence of 87:2-3.
God creates and proportions, joining خَلَقَ to fitness immediately before measuring and guidance.
God measures and guides, فَقَدَّرَ فَهَدَىٰ, placing the section's creation, fitting, and hidaya in one compact sequence.
Moses says the Lord gave each thing its creation and then guided it, making guidance the carrying-forward of a creature's given form and fitness.
Zechariah asks God for good offspring as a gift from Him, closely echoing the couple's request for a ṣāliḥ child in 7:189.
The answer grants John as a son who confirms a word from God, bringing a bestowed child and the ṣ-d-q act of confirmation into the same birth announcement.
Zechariah's prayer not to be left childless frames offspring as a hoped-for divine provision rather than a human entitlement.
God answers, gives John, and repairs his wife for him, explicitly presenting fertility and the child as gifts met by reverent hope and fear.
Abraham's wife strikes her face and calls herself an old barren woman, a birth-announcement face-scene whose cause is impossible fertility rather than contempt for a daughter.
The messengers answer that the wise and knowing Lord has decreed the son, locating the apparently impossible birth within divine measure.
Abraham asks his Lord for a child among the righteous, closely repeating the ṣāliḥ-child request carried by the section from 7:189.
God gives him good news of a forbearing boy, answering the prayer and staging a son as divine glad tidings rather than as human status.
Divorce before touching or fixing a bridal due still requires a fair gift according to means, separating marital giving from consummation.
When a due was fixed but the marriage ends before touching, half remains owed unless freely waived, defining the bridal gift at the boundary of sexual union.
Even a very large bridal gift may not be reclaimed when one wife is replaced by another, protecting the giving that attends marriage.
The prohibition on taking the gift back is grounded in spouses having gone intimately to one another and in the wife's solemn covenant.
Lawful marriage requires seeking women in chastity and giving them their due compensation, another direct Qur'anic formulation of the bridal gift.
A marriage dissolved before touching has no waiting period, yet the woman must be given a provision and released graciously, marking union's legal boundary while preserving giving.
Spouses created from yourselves provide tranquility, affection, and mercy, stating what the section's male-female approach and bridal joining are for.
The Creator makes spouses from human selves and pairs among cattle by which creation multiplies, extending sexual pairing into providential increase.
The pagan rule assigning what is in cattle wombs to males but barring wives, with another rule for stillbirth, exposes arbitrary male-female valuation attached to the womb.
The question whether God forbade the two males, the two females, or what the females' wombs contain dismantles invented sex-based rules by demanding knowledge.
The same male-female-womb interrogation is repeated for camels and cattle, completing the challenge to manufactured gender distinctions.
Faces of wrongdoers seem covered with pieces of dark night, giving literal Qur'anic form to the section's reading of night descending upon the face darkened at a daughter's news.
God desires ease, not hardship, in the fasting passage whose night, marital approach, and dawn are developed two ayat later in 2:187.
The assurance that with hardship comes ease refuses the old formula's permanent assignment of ʿusr to one sex and yusr to the other.
The repeated assurance makes ease accompany the same hardship, reinforcing that these conditions are divinely related rather than biologically gendered.
The buried girl is herself brought forward and questioned, reversing the father's power to hide or erase the unwanted female child.
The question 'for what sin?' declares the girl's innocence and condemns the endpoint of the dark preference staged in 16:58-59.
The question whether males are for the hearers while females are assigned to God exposes their preferred share as a value judgment about the sexes.
Calling that allocation an unjust division explicitly condemns the male-favoring scale that the section hears in the old birth formula.
The question whether God took daughters from what He creates while selecting sons for people exposes their gender hierarchy within the language of creation.
A man receiving the very female child he attributes to God turns dark-faced and choked with grief, repeating and sharpening 16:58's scene.
The next rhetorical description voices the culture's disparaging picture of the female child, allowing the surrounding rebuke to expose how that ranking is constructed.
Calling the angels female is condemned as unwitnessed testimony, separating created sexual categories from invented claims about the unseen.
The question 'daughters for your Lord and sons for them?' directly confronts the same preference for male offspring over female.
The question whether the angels were created female while the claimants watched joins female creation-language to a rebuke of groundless gender attribution.
The question whether God chose daughters over sons lays bare the hierarchy presumed by the speakers rather than accepting it.
'How do you judge?' turns the preceding son-daughter allocation into an indictment of the human value judgment itself.
The question whether God favored people with sons while taking female angels for Himself exposes the contradiction in their preferred-sex theology.
'Daughters for Him and sons for you?' is another concise exposure of assigning the devalued sex to God while reserving the valued sex for oneself.
People fabricate sons and daughters for God without knowledge, while He is exalted above their associations; the Creator of the sexes is not assigned offspring by them.
The Creator of everything is asked how He could have a child without a consort, marking divine creation as categorically beyond the pair-to-birth sequence in creatures.
In the immediate Mary-and-Jesus context, God does not take a son; He creates by decree, bounding the section's ordinary reproductive imagery at divine agency.
'He neither begets nor is begotten' marks the sharp theological boundary between the Creator invoked in 92:3 and the male-female generation He creates.
Calling wives a tilth links marital approach to the possibility of generation, a different bodily figure for the section's movement from covering to pregnancy.
Nursing, the father's provision and clothing, and the ban on harming either parent through the child extend birth into reciprocal duties of giving.
God forms people in wombs however He wills, joining hidden formation and divine choice behind the male-female child.
Marriage to believing bondwomen requires family permission and fair payment of their bridal dues, extending the section's gift obligation across social rank.
A believer who acts rightly, male or female, enters the Garden without injustice, repeating the section's replacement of sex with action as the decisive measure.
Marriage to chaste believing or scriptural women is lawful when their bridal dues are given, again binding union to an actual gift.
When night غَشِيَ Abraham, it literally covers a person; this supplies the ordinary covering sense from which the section hears the verb's sexual usage.
Night rapidly covers day with يُغْشِى, restaging the cosmic cover that the section maps onto marital approach.
Believing men and women are allies who together establish prayer and give alms, putting both sexes on the giving side of the surah's moral divide.
The same believing men and women are promised the same gardens and divine pleasure, completing 9:71's shared action with a shared end.
Night is made for rest and day made visible, a functional night-day pair that supports the section's covering and disclosure pattern.
Abraham's standing wife receives glad tidings of Isaac and then Jacob, staging motherhood and lineage as an unexpected divine announcement.
She asks how she can bear while old and her husband aged, marking the biological limit that the promised birth crosses.
The messengers answer by invoking God's mercy and blessing on the household, interpreting the unlikely child as bestowed grace.
Abraham praises God for granting Ishmael and Isaac despite old age, explicitly receiving sons as gifts rather than achievements or status tokens.
Human creation from a drop supplies another terse formulation of the bodily origin underlying the male-female pair.
People assign daughters to God while reserving what they desire for themselves, setting up the dark-faced daughter announcement in 16:58.
God makes spouses from people's own kind and gives children, grandchildren, and provision, joining pair, offspring, and gift.
Any believer who acts rightly, male or female, receives a good life and reward, making conduct rather than sex the path to good outcome.
The ban on killing children for fear of poverty is grounded in God's provision for child and parent, opposing refusal of the child-gift through anxiety about giving.
Mary guards her chastity, God breathes into her, and mother and son become a sign, preserving the virgin birth as an explicit exception to ordinary coupling.
The Last Hour makes every pregnant woman lay down her load, a catastrophic interruption of pregnancy that marks a boundary to ordinary delivery.
Night is made a garment and day a rising, reinforcing the section's meeting of marital garment, nocturnal covering, and daylight emergence.

The queen's هَدِيَّة is a gift dispatched to a recipient; this may faintly illuminate the h-d-y family's sense of something borne toward another, alongside the bride being led and gifted in the source section.
Solomon refuses the dispatched gift because God's giving is better; with 27:35 this may clarify the difference between human هدِيَّة and divine bestowal, though the bridal link remains indirect.
The Midianite father offers one daughter to Moses in a marriage agreement whose required service functions as the concrete bridal consideration.
Moses accepts the marriage terms as an agreement between the two men, completing 28:27's scene of a bride being joined to her husband.
Knowledge of what is in the wombs belongs to God, reinforcing the section's hidden pregnancy as a domain of divine knowledge.
Human progeny is made from an extract of lowly fluid, another direct account of generation from the sexual drop.
God proportions the human and gives hearing, sight, and hearts, extending reproductive origin into fitted life and the demand for gratitude.
God says He married Zaynab to the Prophet after Zayd's bond ended, giving a direct Qur'anic instance of a woman being joined to a husband.
The Prophet's wives whose bridal dues he has given are named as lawful, tying marital union to completed giving.
God creates all pairs—from the earth's growth, from human selves, and from what people do not know—placing the male-female image in a wider created pattern.
A human created from a drop becomes an open disputant, another sharp juxtaposition of humble reproductive origin and later agency.
God wraps night over day and day over night, a nonlexical version of the reciprocal covering and disclosure that frames the section.
A believer who does right, male or female, enters the Garden and is provided without measure, joining equal moral standing with divine provision.
God makes night for rest and day giving sight, another direct night-day pair structured as cover and visibility.
Dust, drop, clot, emergence as a child, maturity, and old age place birth inside a divinely completed life-course.
God creates pairs of all things and provides ships and cattle to ride, extending paired creation into the gifts that carry creatures to destinations.
God guides and sets right those killed in His way, beginning a sequence in which guidance leads to an actual destination.
God admits the guided into the Garden He has made known to them, concretely realizing hidaya as being brought to arrival.
Abraham is given glad tidings of a knowledgeable boy, opening the scene whose focus then shifts to his barren wife's response.
Creation of all things in pairs universalizes the relational pattern that 92:3 names as male and female.
Believing men and women share light running before them toward one promised end, combining gender parity with illumination after the section's night-day frame.
The emigrant women's former bridal payments are reimbursed and new marriages require new payments, treating the marriage gift as a protected obligation across separation.
Mary's guarded chastity, divine breath, and faithful response repeat the birth without male approach as a boundary case to the section's ordinary reproductive scene.
The exalted majesty of the Lord has neither consort nor child, distinguishing the Most High from the paired and begetting creatures He makes.
God creates the human from a mixed drop for a test and equips him with hearing and sight, joining reproductive formation to moral purpose.
After creating and equipping the human, God guides the way and leaves gratitude or ingratitude as the response, echoing 7:189-190's promised thanks and betrayal.
The command that a human consider what he was created from opens the reproductive examination answered in 86:6-7.
Creation from a gushing fluid names the generative material behind the male-female birth scene.
The fluid's emergence from within the body develops the hidden bodily origin introduced in 86:5-6, though its anatomical wording is distinct from the womb passages.
Creation of the human from a clinging form gives another concise embryonic use of خَلَقَ relevant to the section's formed flesh-piece.
